title: NSW HSC Physics Module 8: From the Universe to the Atom
description: A classroom review organised around the five Module 8 inquiry questions: the origins of elements, atomic structure, quantum atoms, nuclear energy and the Standard Model.
course: NSW HSC Physics — Module 8: From the Universe to the Atom
author: Generated with Classroom Jeopardy Quiz Maker

questions.prompt: What observation provides strong evidence that the early Universe was once hotter and denser than it is today?
questions.answer: The cosmic microwave background radiation.

questions.prompt: The graph shows recessional velocity against distance for several galaxies. What relationship does it display, and what does the gradient represent?
questions.answer: It displays Hubble’s Law, v = H₀d. The gradient is the Hubble constant H₀.
questions.imageAlt: A straight-line graph of galaxy recessional velocity against distance, passing through the origin with gradient labelled H zero.

questions.prompt: Which light nuclei were produced in significant amounts during Big Bang nucleosynthesis?
questions.answer: Mostly hydrogen and helium nuclei, with small amounts of deuterium, helium-3 and lithium.

questions.prompt: The Sun converts 4.3 × 10⁹ kg of mass into energy each second. Using E = mc², estimate its power output.
On the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, identify regions A and B.
questions.answer: A is the red-giant or supergiant region: cool but very luminous. B is the white-dwarf region: hot but dim.
questions.imageAlt: A Hertzsprung–Russell diagram with luminosity increasing upward and temperature decreasing to the right. Region A is upper right and region B is lower left.

questions.prompt: A galaxy recedes at 14 000 km s⁻¹. Using H₀ = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, estimate its distance.
questions.answer: d = v/H₀ = 200 Mpc.

questions.prompt: Explain why ordinary stellar fusion builds nuclei only up to about iron, and how many elements heavier than iron are produced.
questions.answer: Fusion up to iron releases energy because binding energy per nucleon increases. Fusion beyond iron requires energy. Heavier nuclei are formed mainly by neutron-capture processes in evolved stars and explosive events such as supernovae and neutron-star mergers.

questions.prompt: State the charges of a proton, neutron and electron.
questions.answer: Proton: +e. Neutron: 0. Electron: −e, where e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

questions.prompt: The cathode-ray beam bends towards the positively charged plate. What does this show about the beam?
questions.answer: The beam contains negatively charged particles: electrons.
questions.imageAlt: A cathode-ray tube contains a beam travelling right between parallel plates. The upper plate is positive, the lower plate is negative, and the beam curves upward.

questions.prompt: Millikan measured oil-drop charges of 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What elementary charge do these data support?
questions.answer: 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Each measured charge is an integer multiple of this value.

questions.prompt: In Rutherford scattering, most alpha particles passed straight through while a few were deflected through large angles. What two conclusions followed?
questions.answer: Atoms are mostly empty space, and nearly all positive charge and mass are concentrated in a very small, dense nucleus.
questions.imageAlt: Alpha particles approach a thin gold foil. Most continue straight, some deflect slightly and one rebounds through a large angle.

questions.prompt: In a Thomson-style experiment, crossed fields E = 2.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and B = 0.0010 T give no deflection. The electron beam then curves in the same magnetic field with radius 0.114 m. Calculate e/m.
questions.answer: v = E/B, and e/m = v/(Br) = E/(B²r) = 1.75 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹.

questions.prompt: A 5.0 MeV alpha particle approaches a gold nucleus, Z = 79, head-on. Assuming all kinetic energy becomes electric potential energy, estimate its closest approach.
How did Chadwick’s beryllium experiment support the existence of the neutron?
questions.answer: Neutral radiation from beryllium knocked protons from paraffin. Momentum and energy analysis showed the radiation consisted of neutral particles with mass close to a proton’s mass.

questions.prompt: What central assumption did Bohr make about electron energies in atoms?
questions.answer: Electrons can occupy only discrete, quantised energy levels.

questions.prompt: Use the Rydberg equation to calculate the wavelength emitted when a hydrogen electron falls from n = 3 to n = 2. Use R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹.
questions.answer: λ = 6.56 × 10⁻⁷ m, or approximately 656 nm.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows four hydrogen energy levels. Which labelled transition emits the highest-frequency photon?
questions.answer: Transition C, because it has the greatest energy decrease and therefore the largest hf.
questions.imageAlt: Four horizontal hydrogen energy levels are labelled n equals 1 to n equals 4. Three downward transitions A, B and C are shown, with C spanning the largest energy drop.

questions.prompt: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated from rest through 150 V. Use λ = h/√(2meV).
State one major limitation of Rutherford’s atomic model and one limitation of Bohr’s model.
questions.answer: Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability or line spectra. Bohr’s model worked mainly for hydrogen-like atoms and did not fully explain multi-electron spectra.

questions.prompt: The electron intensity graph has sharp maxima as electrons scatter from a crystal. Why did the Davisson–Germer result support de Broglie’s proposal?
questions.answer: The maxima form a diffraction pattern, a wave behaviour. The measured wavelength agreed with λ = h/p, showing that electrons have matter-wave properties.
questions.imageAlt: A graph of scattered electron intensity against angle shows several sharp diffraction peaks. An inset shows an electron beam striking a crystal.

questions.prompt: Calculate the shortest wavelength in the hydrogen Balmer series. Use the limit nᵢ → ∞ and n_f = 2.
questions.answer: λ = 4/R = 3.65 × 10⁻⁷ m, or approximately 365 nm.

questions.prompt: Complete the alpha-decay equation: uranium-238 becomes thorium-234 plus what particle?
questions.answer: A helium-4 nucleus, ⁴₂He, also called an alpha particle.

questions.prompt: A radioactive sample falls from 1600 counts per minute to 200 counts per minute in 18 days. What is its half-life?
questions.answer: 6 days. The activity falls through three half-lives: 1600 → 800 → 400 → 200.

questions.prompt: The separated nucleons for a helium-4 nucleus have total mass 4.03188 u, while the nucleus has mass 4.00151 u. Calculate its total binding energy.
questions.answer: Mass defect = 0.03037 u, so binding energy = 0.03037 × 931.5 = 28.3 MeV.

questions.prompt: Use the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve to explain why both fusion of light nuclei and fission of very heavy nuclei can release energy.
questions.answer: Both processes move nuclei towards the higher binding energy per nucleon near iron, so total binding energy increases and the mass difference is released as energy.
questions.imageAlt: A graph of binding energy per nucleon against mass number rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks near iron and decreases slowly for heavy nuclei.

questions.prompt: In the fission chain-reaction diagram, what role do the released neutrons play, and how is the reaction controlled in a reactor?
questions.answer: Released neutrons trigger further fissions. Control rods absorb excess neutrons, while a moderator slows neutrons to increase the chance of useful fission.
questions.imageAlt: A uranium nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits into two fragments plus three neutrons. Those neutrons travel towards other uranium nuclei, forming a chain reaction.

questions.prompt: Assume each uranium-235 fission releases 200 MeV. Estimate the energy released if 1.0 kg of uranium-235 undergoes complete fission. Use N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
Why must a fusion plasma be extremely hot and confined for long enough, even though the final nuclei are more tightly bound?
questions.answer: Positively charged nuclei must overcome strong electrostatic repulsion before the short-range strong nuclear force can bind them. High temperature supplies kinetic energy, and confinement maintains sufficient density and collision time.

questions.prompt: Give the quark composition of a proton and a neutron.
questions.answer: Proton: uud. Neutron: udd.

questions.prompt: Which Standard Model family contains electrons and neutrinos, and which family contains the constituents of protons and neutrons?
questions.answer: Electrons and neutrinos are leptons; protons and neutrons are made from quarks.

questions.prompt: An up quark has charge +⅔e and an anti-down quark has charge +⅓e. What is the charge of the meson u anti-d?
Name the force carrier for the electromagnetic, strong and weak interactions.
questions.answer: Electromagnetic: photon. Strong: gluons. Weak: W⁺, W⁻ and Z⁰ bosons.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows beta-minus decay at quark level. Which quark changes flavour, and what particles are produced by the intermediate W boson?
questions.answer: A down quark changes into an up quark by emitting a W⁻ boson. The W⁻ becomes an electron and an electron antineutrino.
questions.imageAlt: A down quark changes to an up quark and emits a W minus boson. The W minus decays into an electron and an electron antineutrino.

questions.prompt: A proton circulates in a ring of radius 4300 m in an 8.3 T magnetic field. Using p = qBr and E ≈ pc, estimate its energy in teraelectronvolts.
questions.answer: E ≈ 10.7 TeV.

questions.prompt: A gamma photon produces an electron–positron pair near a nucleus. What minimum photon energy is required, and why is the nearby nucleus important?
questions.answer: At least 2m_ec² = 1.022 MeV. The nucleus recoils so momentum can be conserved.
questions.imageAlt: A gamma ray passes close to a nucleus and converts into an electron and positron whose tracks curve in opposite directions.

finalRound.category: Beta Decay from Nucleus to Quarks
finalRound.prompt: Carbon-14 undergoes beta-minus decay. Write the complete nuclear equation, then describe the decay at quark level and explain how electric charge and lepton number are conserved.
finalRound.answer: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + e⁻ + anti-νₑ. Inside one neutron, a down quark becomes an up quark, changing udd into uud and therefore a neutron into a proton. A W⁻ is emitted and decays into an electron and electron antineutrino. Charge is conserved: 0 → (+1) + (−1), and lepton number is conserved because the electron has +1 and the antineutrino −1.
finalRound.imageAlt: Carbon-14 changes into nitrogen-14 while emitting an electron and electron antineutrino. An inset shows a neutron's down quark changing into an up quark through a W minus boson.
